title: Provincial Disability Programs
subtitle: Compare local disability definitions without mixing the rulebooks

blocks.text: A disability can cross a provincial border. Its benefit file, less adventurous, usually has to stop and ask for directions.

Each province and territory runs its own disability income and health support. Ontario has ODSP. Alberta has AISH and ADAP. B.C. uses a Persons with Disabilities (PWD) status, and Quebec has Social Solidarity plus, for some long-term clients, the Basic Income Program. These are separate programs with their own rules, not local names for one national benefit.
A federal DTC or CPP disability approval can help with some provincial programs, but it does not prove you qualify everywhere. Each program decides which outside approvals it will accept.

items.title: “A disability-benefit approval transfers automatically when a person moves provinces.”
items.text: The condition moves with you. The provincial benefit usually does not. Your new province may ask for a new application, a new disability review and a new money check.

blocks.text: Ontario: ODSP
Knowing which rulebook applies keeps you from losing months to the wrong form.
blocks.detail: Four checks show what your province needs before it pays anything, so you can gather the right papers the first time.
blocks.extra: The four gates in Section 02 turn that check into a short list.

sections.title: Disability Status Is Only One Gate

blocks.text: A medical form opens one gate. These four decide whether it leads anywhere.

items.title: WHERE YOU LIVE AND YOUR AGE
items.text: Check where you live, the youngest age that qualifies, any legal status rules and what changes when youth turn adults or adults turn 65.

items.title: THE DISABILITY TEST
items.text: Read your province’s own test for how long, how severe and how much the condition limits daily life and work. Do not copy CPP disability wording into an ODSP, AISH, ADAP, PWD or Social Solidarity form.

items.title: THE MONEY TEST
items.text: Your income, a partner’s income, savings, trusts, RDSPs, gifts and settlements can each count in a different way. A medical approval alone may not lead to a payment.

items.title: AFTER YOU ARE APPROVED
items.text: Work income, monthly or yearly reports, medical reviews, travel, changes at home and health benefits can all change your support later.

blocks.text: Ontario’s ODSP usually checks both a disability test and a money test. B.C. also keeps PWD status separate from the money test for disability help.
Alberta started ADAP in July 2026 next to AISH, with one shared Disability Income Assistance form. The two programs look at work ability in different ways and treat earnings differently.

items.title: “Once the medical form is accepted, income and assets no longer matter.”
items.text: Most provincial disability income programs still check your money. In some places your status can stay in place while a payment pauses, but check your own province’s rule.

blocks.text: Alberta: Disability Income Assistance

sections.title: Build Your File Around Your Province’s Rules

blocks.text: Start with your province’s current application guide. Sort your papers under its own headings: your health history, how long it will last, treatment, daily tasks, help you need, work ability and outlook. You describe how life is affected. Your doctor or other approved health worker gives the medical proof.
B.C. lets some groups get PWD status through a faster route if another program already approved them. That is a B.C. rule. It does not mean every province accepts every other approval.

Next, build the money file: bank statements, rent or housing costs, income, savings, partner details, trusts, RDSPs, settlements and other benefits. Write the date of the rule beside each number. Ask how a paycheque would change your cash support, your health coverage and your reporting, one at a time.
Work rules differ. Ontario does not count the first $1,000 a month that an ODSP client with a disability earns. B.C. uses a yearly limit instead, which is $16,200 for a single PWD client in 2026.

items.title: “Working always causes immediate loss of disability support and health benefits.”
items.text: Many programs let you keep some earnings, cut support only part of the way or keep health coverage for a while. Report your work honestly, and ask for the math in writing before you turn down a job based on folklore.

blocks.text: Before you apply or change your income, compare five things in your own province: the disability test, the money test, the work rules, the health coverage and the review dates.

sections.title: Marcus and the Approval That Packed Light

blocks.text: Meet Marcus
paragraphs: Marcus Bell gets ODSP in Toronto. His sister finds him a ground-floor apartment in Calgary, close to her and close to a job he can do three mornings a week. He packs his ODSP approval letter and assumes Alberta will change the logo. The letter crosses the country beautifully. The entitlement neglects to book a seat.

Two weeks before the move, he calls Alberta to ask where to send his letter. The worker is kind and clear. Ontario’s approval does not carry over. He has to apply for AISH or ADAP on Alberta’s form, under Alberta’s rules.
Then the dates start to pile up. His last ODSP payment covers May. His pills run out in June. The Calgary rent is due on June 1, and a new application can take months.

A friend tells him to cancel ODSP now and start fresh in Alberta. That feels tidy. Marcus thinks about the gap it would open, with no cheque and no drug coverage in either province. He decides not to cancel anything yet. He tells Ontario his move date, asks both programs what happens in between, and gets their answers in writing.

Alberta’s form asks about his work, so he adds his three mornings a week and the pay. He also learns that his old medical forms do not answer every Alberta question. His Calgary doctor fills in the new form, and Marcus writes his own page on how his days go.

The money does not arrive overnight. But Ontario covers his last month, Alberta’s emergency help covers his pills, and his application is complete the first time. Marcus did not just change the logo. He changed the whole plan, and this time the entitlement booked a seat.

blocks.text: Before you move to another province, call both programs. Ask about end dates, new applications, drug coverage, mobility equipment and emergency help. Do not expect two payment calendars to line up on their own.
What resolved the conflict?
Disability support is set by each province. Check the local disability test, the money test and your plan for the gap before you assume an approval travels with you.
Marcus kept his Ontario support, his pills and his job by asking both provinces before he cancelled anything.
blocks.detail: The same four questions can protect your own income and drug coverage if you move, take work or face a review.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 05 tests whether you can spot the next move.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why might a federal disability approval not settle your provincial claim?
items.detail: Each province decides which outside approvals it accepts. A federal DTC or CPP disability approval can help, but it does not prove you qualify everywhere.

items.title: What four gates belong in the comparison?
items.detail: Where you live and your age, the disability test, the money test and the rules after approval.

items.title: Why keep your medical file and your money file apart?
items.detail: You describe daily life and your health worker gives the medical proof. The money file uses other papers and other rules, and a medical approval alone may not lead to a payment.

items.title: How do work earnings rules differ in Ontario and B.C.?
items.detail: Ontario does not count the first $1,000 a month an ODSP client with a disability earns. B.C. uses a yearly limit, $16,200 for a single PWD client in 2026.

items.title: What should you check before moving to another province?
items.detail: Whether the new province needs a new application, disability review and money check, and how end dates, drug coverage and emergency help work during the move.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Provincial Disability Comparison File

blocks.text: Write short notes only. Keep medical records, bank statements and ID somewhere safe, not in this form.
Quebec’s Basic Income Program can move some long-term Social Solidarity clients over on its own once they have the needed history. It is not a first application for everyone with a disability.

items.title: Disability designation
items.text: Official status from your province that you meet its disability test.

items.title: Financial eligibility
items.text: The income and savings test you must pass to get paid.

items.title: AISH / ADAP
items.text: Alberta’s two disability income programs. They look at work ability in different ways.

items.title: Earnings exemption
items.text: Work income your program does not count before it lowers your support.

items.title: Medical review
items.text: A later check that you still meet the program’s disability test.

quiz.question: True or False: “A disability-benefit approval transfers automatically when a person moves provinces.”

questions: Which province or territory do you live in, or plan to move to? Name its disability program if you know it.
Do you already have a disability approval, such as the DTC, CPP disability or a program in another province? Write “none” if not.
Which papers do you still need for your application? For example, a doctor’s form or proof of rent.
About how much do you earn from work each month? An estimate is fine. Write “$0” if you do not work.
What will you ask your program about work income and health coverage?
What is your next important date, and who can help you? For example, a move date, a review or a renewal.
samples: Alberta. I will apply for AISH or ADAP on the shared form.
Yes, ODSP in Ontario. I also have the DTC.
A new doctor’s form and my Calgary lease.
About $600 a month from part-time work.
How much of my $600 can I keep, and will my drug coverage continue?
I move on June 1. My sister and a disability navigator will help me.
